summary: Describes URN namespaces for identifying objects in the EPCglobal system, which is used for products in commerce and supply chains. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Product barcodes name things. This gives items in the EPCglobal tag system official internet-style names.

questions: what is electronic product code urn
how are supply chain products identified
what is the electronic product code urn
subtitle: Internet-standard names for products and supply chain data

tldr.problem: Supply chains and commerce systems use product identification codes that predate the Internet. These codes need Internet-compatible names so they can be used with web services and data systems.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5134 registers two Uniform Resource Name (URN) namespaces with IANA: 'epc' for identifying physical products, and 'epcglobal' for naming system components. Each namespace has formal structure rules defined in ABNF.
tldr.outcome: EPCglobal, a subsidiary of GS1 (the organization managing global product codes), can now issue formal URNs for products and system components in a way that is compatible with the broader Internet naming infrastructure.

today: RFC 5134 is the formal registration of two URN namespaces with IANA. It remains the basis for how EPCglobal product codes are named in the Internet, and it has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: EPCglobal and Supply Chain Identification
sections.content:
The EPCglobal Architecture Framework is a system for identifying and tracking products as they move through supply chains and commerce networks. It uses sensors, data services, and management systems to record events when products are handled, read, or scanned.

The products in this system are identified using codes that existed long before the Internet: the Global Trade Item Number (GTIN), Global Location Number (GLN), and Serialized Shipping Container Code (SSCC). These codes are managed by GS1, an internationally recognized standards organization that has managed product identification for nearly 50 years. For EPCglobal systems to work fully with modern Internet applications, these existing identification namespaces need to be compatible with URNs (Uniform Resource Names), the Internet standard way of naming things.
sections.eli5: Store barcodes and shipping labels use special numbers to identify products. This RFC gives those numbers official Internet names so computers can look them up and work with them on the web.

sections.title: URNs and Namespaces
sections.content:
A Uniform Resource Name (URN) is an Internet standard for naming things. Unlike a URL (which tells you how to reach something), a URN just gives something a unique name. A URN has the form urn:<namespace>:<specific-id>.

A URN Namespace is a registered identifier that groups related names. For example, urn:isbn: is the namespace for International Standard Book Numbers. This RFC registers two new URN namespaces: urn:epc: and urn:epcglobal:. Each namespace is managed by an organization (here, EPCglobal, Inc.) and can have sub-namespaces for different purposes.
sections.eli5: A URN is like an official name. The first part (before the first colon after 'urn') says what kind of thing it is. The rest is the specific identifier, like a serial number.

sections.title: The EPC Namespace Structure
sections.content:
The urn:epc: namespace is used to name physical objects within supply chains. Its structure is defined as urn:epc:<sub-namespace>:<value>. Sub-namespaces are registered for different product identification systems. The most important is sgtin (Serialized Global Trade Item Number).

An SGTIN URN has the form urn:epc:id:sgtin:<company-prefix>.<product-reference>.<serial-number>. For example: urn:epc:id:sgtin:900100.0003456.1234567. The first part is a company prefix assigned to the manufacturer, the second is a product reference assigned by that company, and the third is a serial number that makes this particular instance unique. Leading zeros are significant and must be preserved.

The structure allows for future sub-namespaces for other identification systems (GLNs, SSCCs, and others) managed by GS1, all under the single urn:epc: namespace ID.
sections.eli5: A product URN has three parts: the company that made it, what product it is, and which copy of that product it is. All three parts are numbers separated by dots.

sections.title: The EPCglobal Namespace for System Components
sections.content:
The urn:epcglobal: namespace serves a different purpose. While urn:epc: names physical things, urn:epcglobal: names logical or software constructs within the EPCglobal system. This includes XML schema namespaces and other technical specifications.

The structure is similar: urn:epcglobal:<sub-namespace>:<value>. An example is urn:epcglobal:ale:xsd:1, which is the XML namespace identifier for the Application Level Events (ALE) Specification. These URNs do not need resolution mechanisms (unlike the urn:epc: namespace, which can be resolved via the Object Naming Service).
sections.eli5: While product URNs name actual boxes and packages, EPCglobal URNs name software parts like data formats and specifications used inside the system.

sections.title: Management, Resolution, and Security
sections.content:
Both URN namespaces are managed by EPCglobal, Inc., a subsidiary of GS1. Assignment of URNs follows EPCglobal's standards publication process. The namespaces are registered with IANA, the Internet organization that manages global identifier pools. Uniqueness is guaranteed by GS1's namespace management experience, and the binding between a name and what it names is permanent.

The urn:epc: namespace supports resolution via the Object Naming Service (ONS), which is based on the Dynamic Delegation Discovery System (DDIS). This allows systems to look up information about a product given its URN. Each sub-namespace has namespace-specific validation rules defined in EPCglobal documentation.

A key security consideration is that these names identify physical objects of potential commercial value. The system relies on digital signatures, secure resolution mechanisms, and trust relationships to prevent spoofing of metadata (such as cost, size, or location) associated with a URN.
sections.eli5: A company controls the official assignment of product URNs, and once assigned, they never change. Computers can look up information about a product using its URN, but security measures prevent someone from faking that information.
